A beginner first learns to hold the mallet tilted slightly to the right, which gives a fuller sound; the other hand holds the previous bar to damp it before the new note is struck, so that the sound does not become muddy, and repeated notes are damped half a beat early. For saron barung and demung it is best to practise playing the core melody from the notation first, and then the interlocking complementary rhythm with instruments of the same type; saron panerus keeps a steady beat and, according to the tempo level, adds repeated notes or paired-note variations.

薩隆為印尼甘美蘭合奏中的體鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號111.2: The saron is an idiophone of the Indonesian gamelan ensemble, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.222. The earliest known image of a single-octave saron appears in ninth-century reliefs at Borobudur. It was once supposed that the saron developed from the gambang gangsa, but Mantle Hood argued against this, holding that the preference for a single octave is connected with the cadential forms of the pathet modes; the evidence available does not show that the gambang gangsa is older than the saron, and the latter may even have appeared later.
薩隆為體鳴樂器，以槌敲擊置於共鳴框上的青銅音條發聲。音量與清晰度主要由右手斜擊角: The saron is an idiophone, sounding by striking with a mallet the bronze bars set on a resonating frame. Volume and clarity are controlled mainly by the angle of the right hand's slanted stroke and by the left hand holding the bar to damp it: a slanted stroke gives a fuller sound, and damping keeps the ring from becoming muddy. Among instruments of the family the range drops with size: the smallest, the panerus, is highest, the barung an octave lower, the demung an octave lower again; the slendro scale usually has six keys, and the pelog scale usually omits the fourth note. The panerus uses a buffalo-horn mallet, which gives a sharper timbre, and usually keeps a steady beat; the barung and demung mostly use wooden mallets, play less and more simply, and mainly present the core melody.

The saron is an idiophone used in the Indonesian gamelan ensemble, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.222. It usually consists of seven bronze bars set on a resonating frame (rancak), about twenty centimetres high, and the player sits on the floor and strikes them with a mallet (tabuh). The pelog scale is usually laid out as 1-2-3-5-6-7 and the slendro scale as 6-1-2-3-5-6-1, and it can differ from set to set; slendro usually has six keys. It provides the core melody (balungan) in the ensemble.
